definition: Equitable means fair and just in a way that accounts for people's different needs or circumstances.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word equitable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know equitable should be able to work it out from your sentence.

An acceptable arrangement is merely good enough, while an equitable one is genuinely fair to people with different needs.
An equitable policy treats people fairly in practice, while a just one meets the highest standard of moral rightness.

Fair is the everyday, all-purpose word for treating people in a reasonable, acceptable way, and it fits any situation from board games to courtrooms. Equitable is fair's formal cousin with a sharper edge: an equitable arrangement takes people's different needs and circumstances into account. Every equitable plan is fair, but casual fairness needs no such calculation.

Balanced means giving appropriate weight to all sides — a balanced news report, a balanced committee. Equitable is about outcomes for people: whether a distribution genuinely serves those with different needs and circumstances. A report can be balanced between two views; only a policy that answers people's unequal situations is equitable.

Equitable means fair and just in a way that accounts for people's different needs or circumstances.
Principal Ramos had one pot of tutoring money and two very different schools to serve.
Instead of splitting it fifty-fifty, she funded three extra tutors at the school where most students had no internet at home, and one at the school where most families already paid for private help.
Some parents grumbled that the split was unequal.
Ramos explained that identical shares would have left the students who needed the most help with the least support, and the board agreed her plan was the more equitable one.
The funding split is equitable because it accounts for the two schools' different needs to reach a genuinely fair outcome, even though the shares are not identical.
Use equitable for policies, distributions, and outcomes that are genuinely fair once people's different needs are taken into account; equal shares are not always equitable shares.
Equitable focuses on fair outcomes, unlike parity, which measures equal levels between two things, or impartial, which describes an unbiased judge or process.

When the district received eight hundred donated laptops, the easy plan was one per classroom, everywhere, identical.
The technology committee rejected it.
Identical, one member argued, was not the same as equitable.
A survey had shown that in two schools nearly every student already had a computer at home, while across town most families shared a single phone.
So the laptops followed the need: the schools with the least home access received the most machines, plus hotspots for students without internet.
A few parents grumbled that even-handed meant identical.
The superintendent answered that handing everyone the same thing, whatever their circumstances, was the tidiest way to leave the gap exactly where it was.
